chunks.text: # My Advice for Junior Students, and My Goals ## Advice I'd give a first-year CS student Ok so, if you're just starting computer science, here's what I'd tell you: - **Don't just memorise definitions or copy code.** It might get you through one quiz, but it won't help you later when the questions change. - **Understand the basics properly.** Variables, loops, functions, tables, keys. Everything later is built on these. - **Practise regularly.** Programming and SQL need way more practice than you think. A little every day beats a lot the night before. - **Build small projects as you learn.** Even a tiny project teaches you how things connect. My DBMS project CaseTrack taught me more than reading about databases ever did. - **Read your error messages.** When code gives an error, read it and try to understand what caused it before you start changing random things. - **Ask questions early.** If you don't get something, ask your teacher, a classmate or even an AI tool, but ask before the confusion piles up. - **Revise before quizzes.** Short revision notes plus a few MCQs work really well. - **Don't compare your progress with everyone else's.** Everyone learns at a different speed. Focus on improving compared to yourself last month. - **Use AI wisely.** It's great for explanations and getting unstuck, but make sure you understand what it gives you. ## My goals Short term, my goal is to get better at programming, databases and full-stack development, make my projects stronger, and become more confident at solving problems independently.

# About Me (Bio) Ok so, I'm Usman Tahir. Most people just call me Usman. I'm a university student in Pakistan, doing my BS in Computer Science (BSCS). I'm still learning, and honestly I like it that way. My studies so far have covered things like database management, SQL, parallel and distributed computing, and assembly language. Each of these subjects showed me a different layer of how computers actually work: databases taught me how data is stored, organised and protected, assembly showed me what happens down at the level of registers and memory, and parallel and distributed computing showed me how big problems get split across many processors or machines. The thing I've spent the most hands-on time on is a university DBMS project called CaseTrack, a Judiciary Management System. The frontend, the backend routes and the database all have to work together, and when one of them breaks, everything breaks. I speak Urdu and English. # Essay: What Learning Computing Has Taught Me So Far I'm a university student learning computer science, and if I had to sum up what my courses have taught me so far, it would be this: a computer system is made of layers, and you only really understand it when you see how the layers talk to each other. Each subject I've studied showed me a different layer. Database management and SQL taught me how information is organised, linked and protected, with tables, keys, queries and permissions. Assembly language in EMU8086 took me right down to the bottom, where a program is just instructions moving values between registers and memory and setting flags. Parallel and distributed computing took me the other direction, to the level where one problem is split across many processors or many machines that need to coordinate. On their own, each of these felt like a separate world. Together, they started to form one picture. The thing that really connected the picture for me was a practical project: CaseTrack, my Judiciary Management System. It uses an HTML, CSS and JavaScript frontend, a Python Flask backend, and a Microsoft SQL Server database. Connecting these parts was not easy. I remember a navigation problem where clicking a section like Cases did not display the expected page. In theory that sounds like a small frontend issue, but in practice I had to trace it through the JavaScript event handlers and the backend routes before I understood what was going on. Working through problems like that showed me that building an application is more than writing code: the frontend, the backend routes and the database operations all have to agree with each other.

I'm still learning, and I know there's a lot I don't know yet. My plan is simple: keep practising, keep building projects, and keep learning from my mistakes. One working feature at a time.

# Project Write-up: CaseTrack - Judiciary Management System ## What CaseTrack is CaseTrack is a Judiciary Management System that I have been building and debugging as my university DBMS project. The idea is simple: courts deal with a lot of connected information, and keeping it on paper or in scattered files makes it hard to find anything. CaseTrack keeps that information in one relational database and gives people a web interface to work with it. The main things CaseTrack manages are users, courts, judges, lawyers and cases. These are naturally related to each other. A case is heard in a court, a judge is assigned to it, lawyers represent the parties, and users of the system need to log in to see or change the records. That web of relationships is exactly why a relational database is a good fit for this kind of system. It is still a project I'm developing and debugging, so I won't call it fully finished. ## The tech stack CaseTrack has three layers: 1. **Frontend:** HTML for the structure of the pages, CSS for the styling, and JavaScript for the interactive parts, mainly navigation between the different sections such as Cases. 2. **Backend:** Python with the Flask framework. Flask receives requests from the browser through routes, runs the logic, talks to the database and sends results back. 3. **Database:** Microsoft SQL Server, which I manage through SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). The tables for the different entities live here, along with the relationships between them.

So I had to learn to debug across layers: check the browser, check the Flask route, then check the query in SSMS.

# My Study Notes (DBMS, SQL Server, EMU8086 Assembly, Parallel and Distributed Computing) These are my own short revision notes from my courses. I write notes like this before quizzes: key points first, then a small example. ## 1. DBMS and SQL in SQL Server **Relational database basics.** Data is stored in tables (relations). Each row is a record, each column is an attribute. A primary key uniquely identifies each row, and a foreign key links a row to a row in another table. In CaseTrack, for example, a case would point to the court it belongs to through a foreign key. **The three kinds of SQL commands I practise the most:** - **DDL (Data Definition Language):** defines the structure. `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP TABLE`. - **DML (Data Manipulation Language):** works with the data inside tables. `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SELECT`. - **DCL (Data Control Language):** controls who can do what. `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `DENY`. Small example in T-SQL: ```sql CREATE TABLE Court ( CourtID INT PRIMARY KEY, CourtName VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, City VARCHAR(50) ); INSERT INTO Court (CourtID, CourtName, City) VALUES (1, 'District Court', 'Lahore'); SELECT CourtName FROM Court WHERE City = 'Lahore'; ``` **Logins vs users in SQL Server.** This confused me at first. A *login* is at the server level: it lets you connect to the SQL Server instance. A *user* is at the database level: it is mapped to a login and decides what you can do inside one specific database. So the usual order is: create the login, create a user for it in the database, then grant permissions to that user.

So the usual order is: create the login, create a user for it in the database, then grant permissions to that user. ```sql CREATE LOGIN student_login WITH PASSWORD = '<choose-a-strong-one>'; CREATE USER student_user FOR LOGIN student_login; GRANT SELECT ON Court TO student_user; ``` **Why access control matters.** In a system like a judiciary database, not everyone should be allowed to change case records. Permissions make sure people can only do what their role needs. **SSMS tip.** I test every query in SSMS on its own before putting it into my Flask code. If the query works in SSMS but fails in the app, the bug is in the app layer, not the SQL. ## 2. Assembly Language with EMU8086 **Registers.** The 8086 has general purpose registers AX, BX, CX and DX (each split into high and low bytes like AH and AL). SI and DI are index registers, SP and BP are for the stack, and CS, DS, SS and ES are segment registers. **Flags.** The flags register stores the result status of the last operation: Zero Flag (ZF) when the result is zero, Carry Flag (CF) for unsigned overflow, Sign Flag (SF) for a negative result, Overflow Flag (OF) for signed overflow. Conditional jumps like `JE`, `JNE`, `JG` and `JC` read these flags. **Addressing modes I need to remember:** - Immediate: `MOV AX, 5` - Register: `MOV AX, BX` - Direct: `MOV AX, [1234h]` - Register indirect: `MOV AX, [BX]` - Based/indexed: `MOV AL, ARR[SI]`

`JE`, `JNE`, `JG` and `JC` read these flags. **Addressing modes I need to remember:** - Immediate: `MOV AX, 5` - Register: `MOV AX, BX` - Direct: `MOV AX, [1234h]` - Register indirect: `MOV AX, [BX]` - Based/indexed: `MOV AL, ARR[SI]` **Loops.** `LOOP` decreases CX by one and jumps back while CX is not zero, so I set CX to the number of repetitions first. Example: sum of an array in EMU8086: ```asm .MODEL SMALL .DATA ARR DB 2, 4, 6, 8 SUM DB 0 .CODE MAIN PROC MOV AX, @DATA MOV DS, AX MOV CX, 4 MOV SI, 0 MOV AL, 0 NEXT: ADD AL, ARR[SI] INC SI LOOP NEXT MOV SUM, AL MOV AH, 4CH INT 21H MAIN ENDP END MAIN ``` **Input/output macros.** Writing a macro for printing a string or reading a character saves repeating the same `INT 21H` setup again and again. Most of my errors in EMU8086 were syntax mistakes and macro errors, so I always check the macro definition first when something weird happens. ## 3. Parallel and Distributed Computing (PDC) PDC is the subject I find the most theory-heavy, with a lot of concepts and architecture topics, so I keep these notes short. - **Parallel computing:** many processors or cores work on parts of one problem at the same time, usually sharing memory, to finish faster. - **Distributed computing:** many separate computers connected by a network cooperate on a task; each has its own memory and they communicate by sending messages. - **Flynn's taxonomy:** SISD (single instruction, single data), SIMD (one instruction on many data items, like GPUs), MISD (rare), MIMD (many independent processors, like multicore CPUs and clusters). - **Shared memory vs distributed memory:** shared memory is easier to program but harder to scale; distributed memory scales better but needs message passing. - **Speedup and Amdahl's law:** the serial part of a program limits how much faster it can get, no matter how many processors you add. - **Common problems:** race conditions, deadlocks, load imbalance and communication overhead. My trick for PDC: link every concept to a real example (a GPU for SIMD, a cluster for distributed memory), because the pure definitions all start to sound the same.
